corrected_value.authors: Tian, J., Braithwaite, D. W., & Siegler, R. S.
corrected_value.title: Distributions of textbook tasks predict student learning: Data from decimal arithmetic.

decisions.location: Section 4 Discussion, lines 1779-1787; see also Section 2 Textbook Content Analyses (Study 1), lines 313-317, 386-404, 628-641, and References, lines 2248-2252
decisions.quote:
The analyses of decimal arithmetic problems in Swiss textbooks match Tian et al.’s findings

(2021) for U.S textbooks (see also Table 2), showing a nonrandom and unbalanced

distribution, too. For instance, in SZB only 12% and in MTB only 16% of addition and

subtraction problems involve decimals with unequal decimal digits, while 32% in SZB and

34% in MTB involve decimals with equal decimal digits.
decisions.reason: In Study 1 (Section 2, 'Textbook Content Analyses (Study 1)') and Section 4 ('Discussion'), Babari, Rütsche, & Schalk (10.23668/psycharchives.21850) explicitly re-test the empirical textbook distribution findings of both Braithwaite & Siegler (2018, 10.1037/xlm0000546, fraction arithmetic in U.S. textbooks, shipped row 456, target_index 0) and Tian, Braithwaite, & Siegler (2021, Journal of Educational Psychology 113(3):516-529, 10.1037/edu0000618, decimal arithmetic in U.S. textbooks, candidate target_index 1). Following Tian et al.'s (2021) coding scheme, the authors analyze 538 decimal arithmetic problems in the Swiss textbook series SZB and 766 decimal problems in MTB, compare their distributions directly against Tian et al.'s (2021) U.S. textbook data in Table 2 and Sections 2.2 and 4, and extend the behavioral test of those decimal textbook biases to Swiss students in Study 2. Tian et al. (2021) is a distinct empirical original paper (different first author, year, journal, and mathematical domain) that is empirically re-tested and absent from the shipped rows. Both listed prior adjudication/state files (d435618b...json and 5c674783...json) are absent.

decisions.quote:
The finding that the fraction problem distributions in Swiss textbooks partly diverge from U.S.

patterns (as identified by Braithwaite & Siegler) provides an additional opportunity to evaluate

the associative learning hypothesis. Given that most Swiss children’s responses in the

Fraction-Test of Study 2 reflected specific patterns in their Swiss textbooks—differing from

the patterns identified in U.S. mathematics textbooks—supports the associative learning

hypothesis. Specifically, in Tasks 1 and 2, when Swiss children saw the operation +/-, they

produced more often two fractions with unequal denominators rather than with equal

denominators. This specific unbalanced presentation of tasks in Swiss textbook is not

present in U.S. textbooks and was not found in U.S. children’s associations. Thus, our results

provide additional empirical support that associations of children reflect their textbook task

pattern rather than inherent features of fraction arithmetic.
decisions.reason: Independent parent full current-body reading supports successful for the specified2018input-dependent associative-learning finding. The authors explicitly design Swiss/U.S.problem-distribution differences to distinguish learned textbook associations from inherent arithmetic preferences, state that the observed Swiss-specific response pattern supports this original claim, and conclude Overall these results complement Braithwaite/Siegler2018. Abstract and GeneralDiscussion describe the two-study conceptual replication positively. Thus differing ambient textbook cell frequencies are the intended cross-context test of the conditional learning claim, not an original requirement that every country reproduce U.S.frequency cells. Table3Task1equal-denominator cross and weak ROPE contrasts remain real source qualifications; its prose describes weak effects in predicted directions and its critical Swiss-specific unequal-versus-equal comparison as supported. Task5is newly added and its unexpected first-option response pattern does not adjudicate a2018task. Exploratory clusters qualify generality without an author whole-target failed/mixed verdict. No inference solely from p-values, effect sizes or a theory being generally plausible is used: both the originally attributed empirical conditional claim and current corresponding pattern are stated. Initial mixed opinion and final schema-invalidsuccessful rationale remain unchanged. This is a new independent raw-source decision, not schema or quote repair; the old final two-attempt budget stays exhausted.
